review: They tried. The game looks pretty (If you're playing on a 4090 like myself), and you can see how the gunplay could have a tiny bit of potential. Fighting the mutants is a nightmare because it is so janky and dumb. They hit you while you're hitting them and it feels terrible. Headshots only remove their heads on normal mode, and their headless bodies still fight you. This makes it pretty awful to fight a group of them. Fighting the A.I. Humans is absolutely terrible. They just pursue you with no intelligence and fire endlessly. If you don't have solid cover, you have to run away or you're eventually going to die. They seem robotic and are just too aimbot-ish. You can tell what the Devs were going for, and it is a cool idea, but sadly they just did not produce something that was quality enough to charge money for. They got my curious $25, and I was not smart enough to play it within the window to get a refund. But in this state of the game, it is not worth the money. Maybe it never will be.

How do you fuck up this bad. review:
TL;DR
I cannot recommend this game at the normal price. There are too many bugs and too few QoL features for being a version 1.0. I still experience crashes at times as well.

This game has some things going for it. Most of them are the similarities to Medieval Dynasty. But where it should be better, it is not. Why are there still so many games without a lot of QoL features? Why can't I hold a button to transfer a whole stack? I need to drag and drop for that?! And why are arrows so bugged? If an enemy is killed, all arrows hit a wall of air where he was last standing... they also don't stay on an enemy, except for the last one. Have fun searching... The AI bugs out at times as well and their bodies sometimes bug out and are barely visible. Also a grid for placing structures would be great (though they have one for the inner spaces, which is nice). Also don't expect a lot of armor/clothing combinations. basically only some head, foot and main gears.

But let's get to the good points:
I like the liberation system
Many skills make it a little more of an RPG
Parrying actually works OK
Fast travelling to some villages

Overall? 
Buy if it is on sale. Maybe 15 Euros for this game in its current state. I will continue playing but also rage at times.

[h2]It's a nice time waster, but not a deep game.[/h2]

[b]GRAPHICS[/b]
I like the low poly style, but the character models are really ugly. The tavern and the environment do look nice, though.

[b]SOUND[/b]
Nothing to write home about. Some AI was used, but I play these games while listening to podcasts / music, so I turn down the in-game sound anyway. 

[b]CONTROLS[/b]
WASD movement, jump button. You click on stuff to get work done. Some jobs are mini-games / QTEs, but they're laughably easy. Wood cutting is a bit janky. The toilet cleaning mini-game is bad, because it's just an unnecessary element of additional tedium (see below). Generally, I don't like QTEs / click timers, because they offer no real mechanical challenge, they just feel stupid. Especially the cooking could be much more interesting. Let players combine ingredients to create special variants of foods. 

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]
It's NOT a management game. There's ZERO economical management. You never really run out of money. As the tavern grows, you get more money, so restocking the shelves always stays on the same difficulty level. Gameplay mostly revolves about completing mundane tasks (preparing food / drinks, fetching wood / water, cleaning). It's a time management game, first and foremost. The core loop is fine, you never run out of stuff to do. But you do have to accept that it's a very simple game. 

[b]PROBLEMS[/b]
The fairy helpers are kinda useless, because the cook / bartender ones always create "normal" quality items. They should be making better items as they level up. The waitress fairy gets stuck at times. The dishwashing one works fine.

The main issue of this game really is the tedium. Many gameplay elements solely exist to annoy you. Cleaning is the most obvious one. The game turns into "footprint remover simulator" in the later stages, as the fairies do most of the other jobs - unless you insist on creating perfect food / drink items. 

There are some "special" encounters (beggar, traveller) and some funny interactions (people passing out, thievery), but these are only interesting for like 2-3 times. Then they start to be annoying. The map contains some secrets, but it feels like there could be so much more. Maybe they'll add additional elements with future updates.

There's also some padding, especially level 8 is insane. You'll end up with more than 4x the money you actually need to level up and buy all the upgrades. This needs to be rebalanced. I really don't get why you have to meet arbitrary requirements like "sell 30 soups & 30 steaks". It feels unnatural and forced. In my opinion, this "quest" system doesn't offer any real challenge. It would be much better if there was more emergent gameplay. Challenges should be created by interacting systems (cleanliness of the tavern, service / food quality, and so on). There's already a reputation meter (which basically is an XP system), so unlocking the next tavern level doesn't need an additional layer of requirements. 

The prices of food / drink items are predetermined, you have no influence on them. It would be nice to have at least some kind of control over them. Low prices could attract more peasants with more lenient quality requirements, high prices mean that you have to be a great bartender / cook to keep the rich people coming.

Decoration is utterly meaningless right now, it doesn't really affect client quality. Tavern Master does this MUCH better.

Oh, and please add a way to auto-supply water to the washing / cooking stations in the late game. Running to the well is just... well, you know... tedious.

[b]SUMMARY[/b]
It's good for what it is, but it could be SO much better. It's a shallow game, so I can't quite recommend it. I've had some fun, but there's zero replayability.

It's ambitious, and it has a message. I didn't hate my time with it. But for this price tag, the gameplay is too shallow, the experience is too short, and the message about AI is insufficiently developed. If I paid 99 cents for two and a half hours of making the number go bigger, then this would be a thumbs up. But the game costs eight dollars, you can count the number of meaningful upgrades on your hands and toes, and the game doesn't offer any insights or predictions about the current AI situation beyond "AI power usage contributes to global warming" and "Carbon credits are greenwashing."

Even in-universe, the game does a poor job of illustrating the effects of climate change. When it's 45 degrees celsius and the game shows me stock footage of trees burning, that visualization is effective once or twice. They show that stock footage dozens of times, and I already know the planet is on fire when it says the world is 90 degrees celsius. Frankly, it feels like the game is incomplete because the ending is terrible, and there are no more upgrades to unlock after the first hour or so anyway. You just keep grinding the number bigger until everyone dies, I guess. With more work this game could be a gem, but right now it's overpriced for a clicker that starts off strong and then peters out very quickly.
